| Poverty rate | 22.4% | 19.0% | 17.3% | 14.7% | 12.1% | 11.1% |

Official poverty rate, all people. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, Historical Poverty Tables, Table 2.

stem: What is the most important limit on using this table alone to judge the Great Society?

options.text: The table covers too many years to be useful
options.misconception: The span of years is what lets a reader see the change; it is not a limit.

options.text: The table shows the fall but not what caused it
The table hides the fact that poverty rose in 1966
options.misconception: The table shows the rate falling in 1966, from 17.3 percent to 14.7 percent.

options.text: The table counts only people over 65
options.misconception: The table counts all people, not only those over 65.

rationales.A: The span of years is what shows the change over time; it is not a limit on the table.
rationales.B: A table of rates over time shows when poverty fell, but it cannot show which cause did the work.
rationales.C: The table shows the rate falling in 1966, from 17.3 percent to 14.7 percent.
rationales.D: The table gives the official poverty rate for all people, not only for people over 65.
rationales.general:
1. The table gives one number per year: the share of Americans in poverty.
2. Those numbers show when the fall happened and how fast it ran.
3. They say nothing about why it happened: programs, jobs, or a growing economy could all play a part.
4. The table alone therefore cannot prove the Great Society caused the fall.
Remember: A trend shows when; it never shows why by itself.
